newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Opposition NZ First proposes to slash immigration.
newsitem.headline: Opposition NZ First proposes to slash immigration.

text.p: New Zealand First Party leader Winston Peters placed race and immigration firmly on New Zealand's election agenda when he said on Thursday that immigration should be slashed.

Peters, one of the country's most popular politicians, told a meeting of mainly elderly supporters in Pakuranga, in the heart of Auckland suburbia, that NZ First's policy was aimed at stemming the "recent flood of immigrants".

New Zealanders go to the polls on October 12 in their first election under a German-style mixed proportional system that has replaced the British-style, first-past-the-post system. The economic nationalist NZ First rates just behind the governing National Party and even with the main opposition Labour Party.

Peters cited official figures showing immigration had ballooned to 55,000 in the year to June from 24,000 in 1990, or by a total of more than 200,000 over the six-year period. The government in June revised its immigration policy to allow in 35,000 immigrants a year.
Unveiling New Zealand First's policy, Peters said he would trim the numbers by 80 percent to 10,000 annually.

Peters accused some immigrants of "abusing New Zealand's hospitality" and said there was anecdotal evidence to suggest that many recent migrants continued their main business activity back in their countries of origin after gaining residency.

"It is a way of insuring their prospects against any international upset in their areas of business or professional activity and also a way of ensuring that their chidren have free access to New Zealand's public education and/or health system.
"That is not commitment. It is clear abuse of New Zealand's immigration system and of this country's generosity and hospitality," Peters said.
Early this year Peters first raised the issue of immigration in a speech to a meeting in Howick, a popular destination for Asian immigrants and not far from Pakuranga's border.
His popularity has since soared and while off recent peaks, NZ First continues to rate at 20 percent, behind the National Party's 35 percent and on par with Labour's 19 percent.
Political opponents have accused Peters of "playing the race card" to boost his party's support in the October 12 election.
But Peters denied his policy was racist or anti-Asian.
"I didn't mention Asians at all today. I never have," he said after his speech.
Political commentators say NZ First's support would make the party a significant force after the election.
Peters said the "political firestorm" created by his Howick address was irrational.
"New Zealand has neither the social infrastructure, nor the balanced economy, to support the escalation of new arrivals."
Peters quoted an Auckland newspaper report that said hospitals were starting to balk at the number of overseas patients obtaining free hospital care. He suggested medical screening for some visitors.
He also blamed immigration for fuelling inflation as pressure came on the housing sector, particularly in Auckland.
